The job

Blocking, then bolt straight through

Your ceiling is drywall on 2x6 joists about 16″ apart. The Clevo wants bolts 271⁄8″ apart and was designed for concrete, so nothing lines up. Add short 2x6 blocks between the joists from the attic, then bolt right through — drywall, wood, nut on top.

Bolt lines

271⁄8″689 mm apart, along the joists

Holes per side

4at 33⁄16″ · 91⁄2″ total span

Bolts

⅜″ × 7″½″ will not fit — holes are 11.4 mm

Offset

19⁄16″slide off the joist centreline
Why the offset

Four holes at 33⁄16″ pitch step straight over a 1½″ joist — centre the unit and nothing hits solid wood. Slide it 19⁄16″ and one bolt per side lands dead centre in the joist. The other three go into blocking.

What the words mean
Joist
The beams holding your ceiling up. Yours are 53⁄8″ × 1½″, about 16″ apart.
Bay
The hollow gap between two joists. Yours are 14″ and 143⁄8″.
Blocking
2x6 offcuts wedged across a bay to give you solid wood to bolt into.
On edge
Standing the 2x6 up tall, not flat. Same board, seven times stiffer.
Rail
The folded top lip of the module's steel sides, with the bolt holes in it.
A35
A galvanised steel angle bracket. Two hold each end of each block to the joists.
Snap a line
Stretch a chalk-coated string tight between two marks, lift it straight off the surface and let go — it slaps down and leaves a dead-straight line. Over the 3–4 ft you need here, a long straightedge and a pencil does the same job.
Pilot hole
A small locating hole, drilled first. Here they are sightlines: you drill them from the room so you can find the exact spots from the attic.
Clear span
How far a joist reaches unsupported, wall to wall — not the board's length. A joist resting on a wall at each end of a 14 ft room has a 14 ft clear span. Longer span, more bounce.
Setting out

Drill plan

  • Find the centre joist, confirm it with a fine pilot hole, and snap its centreline. Measure everything from that line.
  • Mark the two bolt lines 271⁄8″ apart along it, then step 33⁄16″ across for the rest.
  • Check against the paper template in the box before you drill: it should read 689 × 242 mm.
Shopping list

Buy

Do not use the fischer anchors in the box. Keep them — they are the right fixing if you ever move the unit to a concrete ceiling or a masonry wall. They are the wrong fixing here, for three separate reasons.

Why not the supplied anchors and screws

1. As delivered, six of the eight holes have nothing behind them. Your joists sit 16″ apart; the mounting holes sit 271⁄8″ apart. Only two land on solid timber. The other six sit over open bay — ½″ of drywall, then air. That on its own rules out fitting it as supplied.

2. Adding blocking does not rescue them. This is the part worth understanding, because once your blocks are in there is wood behind all eight holes, and the obvious thought is that the supplied anchors should now work. They still don't, because a fischer SXRL is an expansion plug: a nylon sleeve that grips by being wedged outward against a hard hole wall. That mechanism needs concrete.

  • In softwood there is no hard hole wall. The sleeve simply compresses the fibres, and the radial pressure that creates the grip bleeds away — then keeps bleeding away, because compressed wood creeps for months.
  • In wood the plug makes the fixing weaker, not stronger. You need a plug in concrete because a screw cannot cut threads in concrete. In wood the screw threads bite the fibres directly. Putting a nylon sleeve in between swaps a wood-thread grip for a nylon-on-crushed-wood friction grip. If you were going to use the supplied screws at all, the first thing you would do is throw the plugs away.
  • Your blocks are 1½″ wide. An 11 mm hole down the centre leaves about ½″ of wood each side, and an expanding plug is mechanically a wedge. In a narrow piece that is also working in bending, that is precisely how you split it. A bolt sitting in a clearance hole pushes outward with zero force.
  • Campus and pull-up moves are cyclic shock loads. A friction grip in timber wallows its hole; a clamped joint does not care.

3. Clevo scope them to concrete themselves. Manual p. 7: the supplied screws and plugs are „für Betondecken geeignet“ — suitable for concrete ceilings — and the unit may only be fitted to solid ceilings. There is no published timber value for an SXRL because it is not a timber anchor.

And the upgrade costs almost nothing. A screw driven up into wood is held by its threads, and hanging on it pulls it straight back out — withdrawal, the weakest way to load a screw. A bolt passes right through with a nut on top: the timber is clamped, not gripped, and to fail it has to crush the wood under the washer or snap the steel. You are already in the attic fitting the blocking, so a washer and a nut is one extra minute per bolt and about $20 the lot. You also get something you cannot otherwise have — a fixing you can put a spanner on and check. A plug slowly creeping loose above your ceiling gives you no warning at all.

Not sold there: a crash pad. Use a folded mattress or a bouldering pad from a climbing shop.

Already own it? Drill (corded, or 18V with the side handle fitted — a ½″ bit in framing can grab and wrench your wrist), impact driver, 9⁄16″ socket and a 9⁄16″ spanner, tape, pencil, speed square, a 4 ft level or any straight edge, headlamp, and a plank to kneel on.

Getting the wood cut

Do not have the store cut your blocks to final size. Ask them to cut the 8-footer in half so it fits in the car, and cut the blocks yourself afterwards.

Two reasons. A store saw is accurate to maybe ⅛″ on a good day, and you want these within 1⁄16″ so they wedge in. More importantly you do not yet know the real bay widths — you measure those in the attic with the insulation pulled back, and they vary bay to bay and along their own length. Cut each block a hair long, then tap it in.

Both Home Depot and Lowe's cut lumber free (Home Depot is usually two free cuts, then about 50¢; it varies by store), and neither is precise enough for this. For the four real cuts, a $15 hand saw and a speed square is genuinely enough on a 2x6 — a circular or mitre saw is faster but there is no case for renting one to make four crosscuts.

Drilling — which bit, which direction

Fourteen holes in total, in four batches. Only one bit has to be long, and only one batch is drilled from the attic.

BatchBitWhere you standDepth
On hole size, and on drilling your joist

½″ is a touch generous for a ⅜″ bolt. It is the right call anyway: spade bits jump straight from ⅜″ to ½″, so 7⁄16″ is hard to buy, and the bolt here is loaded in pure tension under fender washers — nothing bears sideways on the hole, so the clearance is structurally irrelevant. The slack even helps you line eight holes up at once. Use 7⁄16″ if you happen to find it.

Be clear-eyed about the two joist holes, though: a ½″ hole through a 1½″ joist takes away a third of its width at that point. For a ceiling joist carrying drywall and light attic storage, tied to its neighbours by the new blocking, that is fine. If your joists are doing anything more — a floor above, a knee wall, a long span — get someone to look before you drill them.

Why the deep holes get drilled downward

Running a ½″ bit 53⁄8″ straight up over your head is genuinely hard — no weight behind the drill, chips in your face, and a bit that wanders. Wander in a 1½″ joist is exactly what you cannot afford. From the attic you stand over it, put your bodyweight behind the drill and can see that it is vertical. Same for the blocks: drill them lying flat on the deck before you fit them, never overhead afterwards.

Build

Order of work

    Before you drill

    Five things

    • Measure the joist span. Under ~12 ft, build as drawn. 12–16 ft, site it nearer a wall. Over ~16 ft, get someone to look at it. Closer to a supporting wall is always stiffer.
    • Blocks must sit flush with the joist bottoms. Check with a straightedge — joists crown, and a block 1⁄16″ proud holds the rail off the ceiling.
    • Snug the nuts, don't crush the drywall. Firm, then stop.
    • Stop if you find grey pebbly loose fill (possible asbestos) or ceramic-knob wiring. Neither is DIY.
    • Attic rules. Early morning, plank across the joists, headlamp, P100 mask and goggles for the insulation. Reinstate it flat, facing down.
